name: Nuremberg Castle (Kaiserburg)
label: Kaiserburg
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/31013768: the OpenStreetMap point 'Imperial Castle'.
notes: Imperial castle on the sandstone rock above the old town.

text.description: Nuremberg Castle is a group of medieval fortified buildings standing on a sandstone ridge above the historical centre. It is made up of the Imperial Castle (Kaiserburg), the former Burgraves' castle and the buildings added later by the city. The ridge setting is what makes it photograph so well: walls, towers and rooflines climb above you in layers, so even a quick snap feels dramatic. The first fortified buildings appear to date from around 1000, and for centuries German kings and emperors stayed here. Look for the round Sinwell Tower, a main keep from the later 13th century that was raised by a floor in the 1560s, and the Heathens' Tower beside the Imperial Chapel, a Romanesque double chapel built around 1200. Much of the castle was ruined in the air raids of 1944/45, and rebuilding took about thirty years, so what you see is a careful restoration. From the phone icon on the map, the castle is only a short step away, so you are shooting up at the walls rather than across at them. Take one wide shot to show the whole mass of stone, then move closer and pick out details such as tower tops, gateways and timber-framed corners. Keep your phone steady against your body or a wall, and check that the towers are not leaning by using the gridlines.
text.geographic_location: In Nuremberg, Bavaria, on a sandstone ridge that rises above the historical centre (the old town). The castle overlooks the old town's streets and rooftops.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so start from Nuremberg's old town and walk towards the castle ridge. The usual way up is along Burgstrasse, which ends right in front of the sandstone ridge. The phone icon on the map is about 35 m south-west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the walls and towers close up, then switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural view. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the tower tops and roof details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 35 m south-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north-east.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line up a tower or wall edge with a vertical line so the buildings do not seem to lean. Tilt the phone up only slightly, or step back, to keep the vertical lines straighter. For a second picture, zoom in on a single tower or gateway and let the sandstone fill the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the sky or the brightest stonework to focus, then lower the exposure slider a little so the sky does not turn white and the stone keeps its colour. If your phone has a panorama mode, you can try it along the base of the walls, but hold still and move slowly.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft morning or late-afternoon light usually flatters the sandstone better than harsh midday sun, and earlier in the day is often quieter.

text.access_note: The castle is a visitor site with parts that may need tickets and have set opening times, so check the official site before you go.

name: Nazi Party Rally Grounds Documentation Center
label: Rally Grounds
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Dutzendteich' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Dutzendteich' (relation/18736108): edge nearest the subject (3271 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/250148138: the OpenStreetMap point 'Documentation Center Nazi Party Rally Grounds'.
notes: Unfinished Congress Hall with the documentation center.

text.description:
The Documentation Center sits inside the north wing of the Congress Hall, a huge, unfinished building left over from the Nazi party rallies. It is a museum about how those rallies were staged and what they led to. The Congress Hall was planned to hold 50,000 people but was never completed. The Austrian architect Günther Domenig won the 1998 competition for the museum with a bold idea: a diagonal glass-and-steel passageway driven through the northern end of the old building. It was unveiled on 4 November 2001. The contrast between the heavy curved stonework and the sharp, modern wedge is what makes the building so striking in a photo.

The main shot is taken from a point about 65 m north-west of the Documentation Center, looking south-east at it, so the glass wedge and the stone hall sit together in one frame. An alternative is the public shore of the Dutzendteich, a park with a lake shore facing the Congress Hall. From there the arched hall, the glass wedge and open sky can fit in one frame, and the lake gives a calm foreground and, on still days, may give a reflection. If you want to see the wedge close up, another viewpoint at the museum entrance shows the glass cutting into the stone facade from below. Another option is the Große Straße, the wide, straight axis of the former rally grounds.

The subject is a serious one, so photograph with respect and keep out of the way of other visitors. The museum has been rebuilding and running an interim exhibition, so check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: The Documentation Center is in the former Nazi Party Rally Grounds in Nuremberg, inside the north wing of the Congress Hall. The Dutzendteich is a public park with a lake shore facing the Congress Hall.
text.directions_text: There is a tram stop by the entrance. Check a local journey planner for the current route. If you would rather try the Dutzendteich shore as an alternative, walk along the public shore until you can see the curved Congress Hall across the water. Check the museum's official site for current access and any building work. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) so the glass wedge and the surrounding hall fit in the frame. Switch to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the glass-and-steel wedge against the stone. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you are close to the building and want to show its scale, and keep the horizon level.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Dutzendteich (lake shore across the water from the Congress Hall). The curved, arched Congress Hall with the Documentation Center's glass-and-steel wedge, seen across the lake under open sky.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the glass wedge off-centre, with the building along the upper line. Keep the phone level so the arches do not lean. If you shoot from the lake shore, place the water in the bottom third. For another view, take a close, upward shot of the glass entrance at the museum, or a long straight view down the Große Straße.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the building to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky keeps its detail and the glass does not blow out. Hold the phone steady with both hands, or rest it on a rail or wall, to keep the shot sharp.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: If you try the lake shore, on still days the water may give a reflection.

text.access_note: The Dutzendteich shore is a public park, but access to the museum and its entrance area may be ticketed or restricted, so check the official site before you go.

name: Nuremberg Trials Memorium
label: Nuremberg Trials
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/1529939905: the OpenStreetMap point 'Memorium Nuremberg Trials'.
notes: Courtroom 600 of the Nazi war crimes trials.

text.description: The Memorium Nuremberg Trials is a museum inside the Palace of Justice, the courthouse where the Nuremberg Trials were held between 1945 and 1949. It is a working piece of history rather than a pretty viewpoint, and that is what makes it worth a photo: a large, formal courthouse building with a serious story behind it. The permanent exhibition opened on 21 November 2010 in the attic of the east wing, directly above Courtroom 600. Since March 2020 that courtroom has no longer been used for court hearings and is part of the museum, so it is open to museum visitors. Outside, the best pictures are of the building itself: its long, strong lines suit a wide shot, and a few steps back lets you fit in more of the facade. Use the gridlines to keep the vertical edges straight, because tilting the phone upwards makes a tall building lean. Then move in and use zoom for details such as doorways, signs and stonework, which tell the story without needing the whole building in frame. Photography rules inside a museum can differ from room to room, and Courtroom 600 is a historic space that is now part of the museum exhibition, so ask staff or check the official site before you go. Be respectful of other visitors, and avoid taking pictures that put strangers in the foreground.
text.geographic_location: In Nuremberg, at the Palace of Justice courthouse, which houses the Memorium Nuremberg Trials museum.
text.directions_text: No tram or Underground stop is listed for this spot, so start from the centre of Nuremberg and head for the Palace of Justice (the courthouse that contains the museum), by taxi or hired scooter. Once you reach the building, the phone icon on the map is at the museum itself, so there is no further walk. Check the official museum site for the visitor entrance before you set off. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the whole building from close range, then switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural look. Use the telephoto/zoom (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for architectural details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. If you need more of the facade in the frame, take a few steps back from the building while keeping the courthouse in view.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line up the building's vertical edges with them so it doesn't lean. Take one wide shot of the whole building, then a closer detail shot of a doorway or sign. Portrait mode is better kept for a person standing in front of the building than for the building itself.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the building to focus, then lower the exposure slider slightly if the sky is bright, so the stonework keeps its detail. If you take photos indoors, check the museum's rules first, and switch off flash.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft, even daylight, such as a bright overcast day, is kind to a large stone building. In sunshine, check the light on the facade when you arrive and wait for it to reach the front.

text.access_note: This is a museum in the historic Palace of Justice, so check the official site before you go for visiting arrangements and photography rules inside.

name: Germanisches Nationalmuseum and Way of Human Rights
label: Germanisches Museum
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Straße der Menschenrechte' (4 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Straße der Menschenrechte' (node/94977274): point.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/56430: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Germanisches Nationalmuseum' (267 m across).
notes: Large cultural-history museum with the column avenue of human rights.

text.description: The Germanisches Nationalmuseum is Germany's largest museum of cultural history, founded in 1852. Its entrance hall opens onto Kartäusergasse, which the Israeli sculptor Dani Karavan turned into the Way of Human Rights (Straße der Menschenrechte). For a phone photo, the street is the better subject. A row of tall concrete columns, 27 in all, leads the eye towards the museum's glass-and-sandstone frontage, with open sky behind. The museum itself is a patchwork of buildings from different periods and grew from the remains of a medieval charterhouse (Kartäuserkloster). The glass entrance hall on this street is part of the large extension of 1988 to 1993, designed by Jan Störmer. That mix of old and new is why the scene works so well: strong repeating verticals in the foreground and warm stone beyond. The street is open-air, so you can take your time. If you go inside, look for signs about photography, because some exhibitions restrict it.
text.geographic_location: In the south of Nuremberg's historic city centre, between Kornmarkt and the medieval city wall along Frauentormauer. The Way of Human Rights is the street, Kartäusergasse, running up to the museum entrance.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so start from the historic city centre and go to its southern side. Head for Kartäusergasse, next to the museum entrance, and look for the row of tall columns. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to get the whole row of columns and the museum front in one frame. Then switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural view, and to the telephoto (2x-3x, depending on your phone) to bring the museum closer and pack the columns together.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Straße der Menschenrechte (north end, by the information panel listing the 27 columns). A row of tall white concrete columns leading toward the museum's glass-and-sandstone frontage, with the sky behind them.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on gridlines and place yourself in line with the row so the columns march away evenly towards the museum. Keep the phone level so the columns stay upright. For a second picture, move closer to the museum for its arched glass front against the pale sandstone, with the columns rising at one side. Kornmarkt gives a quieter view of the older museum block, but the entrance has since moved to Kartäusergasse, so it may be less rewarding today.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the columns to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little if the sky looks washed out. Portrait mode is not needed here, but a quick Live Photo can catch passers-by walking along the row.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or later in the afternoon is likely to be calmer, with fewer people between you and the columns.

text.access_note: The Way of Human Rights is an open-air street where photography is permitted; for the museum interior, check the official site before you go, and look at signs on photography, as flash and tripods are not allowed and some exhibitions restrict photos.

photo.artist: The original uploader was Keichwa at German Wikipedia.

name: Hauptmarkt and Beautiful Fountain
label: Hauptmarkt & Brunnen
camera_source: Stand-here point set at the correction gate (own photo GPS 2026-11-16).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/1499315172: the OpenStreetMap point 'Beautiful Fountain'.
notes: Main market square with the golden Gothic fountain.

text.description:
The Beautiful Fountain stands on the Hauptmarkt, Nuremberg's main market square, right beside the town hall. It is shaped like a Gothic spire, and at about 19 metres high it rises well above the market stalls and the people around it. That height is what makes it easy to photograph: the pointed stonework reads clearly against the sky, and the busy square gives a lively setting around it. The fountain was built by Heinrich Beheim between 1385 and 1396, and it is counted among the main attractions of the city's Historical Mile. During World War II it was surrounded by concrete to protect it from bombing, which is a nice detail to mention if you are sharing the picture with friends.

Use that to your advantage: tilt the phone upwards and let the spire fill the frame, or step back a little and include the market square around its base. Because the fountain is tall and narrow, a portrait (upright) orientation usually suits it best. If you want the surrounding buildings as well, switch to landscape and use the ultra-wide lens (0.5x), keeping the phone level so the spire does not lean.
text.geographic_location: The fountain is on the Hauptmarkt, the main market square in Nuremberg, next to the town hall.
text.directions_text: Make your way to the Hauptmarkt, the main market square beside the town hall. If you are coming from further out, a taxi to the Hauptmarkt is the simplest option. The phone icon on the map is about 15 m south of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for a natural view of the fountain. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want the whole spire and the square in one shot, or to the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the carved details higher up.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 15 m south of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north. Close to the base you will need to tilt up; take a few steps back if the top gets cut off.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Hold the phone upright and turn on the gridlines. Line the spire up with a vertical grid line so it stands straight. Keep a little sky above the tip. For a second picture, turn to landscape and include the market square and nearby buildings for a sense of place.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the stonework to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky is bright, so the detail in the fountain is not washed out. Keep the phone level to reduce leaning verticals, especially with the ultra-wide lens.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early in the morning there are usually fewer people on the square, which makes a clean shot of the fountain easier. Soft daylight on a bright, slightly overcast day also shows the stonework evenly.

text.access_note: The fountain stands on an open public market square; if the market is on, stalls may affect your view, and for any special events check the official site before you go.

name: St. Lorenz Church
label: St. Lorenz
camera_source: Stand-here point set at the correction gate (own photo GPS 2026-11-16).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/144721691: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'St. Lawrence Church' (105 m across).
notes: Twin-towered Gothic church on Lorenzer Platz.

text.description: St. Lorenz (St. Lawrence) is a medieval church in Nuremberg, once a free imperial city. It is one of the most prominent churches of the Evangelical Lutheran Church in Bavaria. It was badly damaged in the Second World War and later restored. It photographs well because the west front is so richly detailed. Two tall towers frame a sharply pointed portal, and above it sits a rose window 9 metres across. The nave was finished around 1400. Work on the hall-style choir began in 1439 in the late German Gothic style known as Sondergotik, and the choir was largely complete by 1477. Inside are a carving of the Angelic Salutation by Veit Stoss and a monumental tabernacle by Adam Kraft, which includes a figure of the sculptor himself. Wealthy citizens looked after the church, which is probably why these works survived the Reformation. For a phone photo, the church is large and the streets around it are fairly tight, so your main decision is how much to include. Start with the whole front, towers and all, then move in on the portal and the rose window. Keep your phone upright for the towers and use the gridlines to keep the verticals straight. If people are walking through the frame, wait a moment or include them to show the scale.
text.geographic_location: St. Lorenz is a church in Nuremberg, in southern Germany.
text.directions_text: No tram or railway stops are listed for this spot, so start from central Nuremberg and head for the twin towers of St. Lorenz, or go by taxi or hired scooter and ask for St. Lorenz church. The phone icon on the map is about 10 m west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Begin with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit both towers and the portal in one shot. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural view, and use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the rose window and the carved doorway.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 10 m west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face east. From here you are looking at the west front, with the two towers, the portal and the rose window.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line up the towers with the vertical lines, holding the phone level so they don't lean. Keep the portal in the centre and leave a little sky above the tower tops. Then take a closer second shot of the rose window with the telephoto lens.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the sky or the pale stonework to set focus, then lower the exposure slider a little so the sky keeps its colour and the stone keeps its detail. If the stone looks too dark, tap on the shaded part of the facade instead.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Try the afternoon or early evening, when sunlight is likely to fall on the west front. At dusk, night mode can capture the lit facade, but brace your arms against something steady.

text.access_note: St. Lorenz is a working place of worship, so check the official site before you go for visiting times and any rules about photography or dress inside.

name: St. Sebaldus Church
label: St. Sebaldus
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Albrecht-Dürer-Platz' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Albrecht-Dürer-Platz' (way/31823653): middle (85 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/139460727: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'St. Sebald Church' (93 m across).
notes: Oldest of the big old-town churches, with the shrine of St. Sebald.

text.description: St. Sebaldus Church is one of the oldest and most important churches in Nuremberg, and it sits on Albrecht-Dürer-Platz in front of the Old Town Hall. It is named after Sebaldus, an 8th-century hermit and missionary who is the city's patron saint. Building began in 1225, and the church was finished by about 1273–75 as a Romanesque basilica with two choirs. The late Gothic hall chancel and the taller steeples came in the 14th and 15th centuries. It was badly damaged in the Second World War and later restored. It photographs well because the dark sandstone walls and twin towers fill the frame, and the Old Town Hall next to it gives the classic postcard composition. Albrecht-Dürer-Platz, in front of the church, gives the west façade with the Old Town Hall beside it. Start wide, then step closer for details. One sculpture, the antisemitic Judensau relief from the 1380s, is about 7 m up on the exterior. You may prefer to leave it out of your frame, or include it deliberately. For a quieter alternative, Winklerstraße shows the church's side and the carved stone oriel of the rectory opposite. Rathausplatz gives a wider view from the town hall side.
text.geographic_location: St. Sebaldus Church stands in Nuremberg's Old Town, on Albrecht-Dürer-Platz, directly in front of the Old Town Hall.
text.directions_text: Head for the Old Town in Nuremberg and aim for the old city hall; by taxi or hired scooter is simplest if you are coming from further out. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) for the postcard view of the church with the Old Town Hall beside it. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if the towers will not fit from the square. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for stonework and sculpture details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Albrecht-Dürer-Platz (in front of the church, facing the west façade). The church's exterior framed with the Old Town Hall beside it, the classic postcard composition.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line up the church's vertical edges with them. Hold the phone level, because tilting it upwards makes the towers lean. Keep the Old Town Hall at one edge of the frame so the two buildings sit together. If the square is busy, try Rathausplatz for a wider street-level view, or Winklerstraße for a quieter angle on the church's side.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the stonework to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little if the sky is bright, so the sandstone keeps its detail. Live Photos can help you pick a moment with fewer people in front of the church.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft morning or late-afternoon light is usually kinder to the stone, and early in the day the square is likely to be quieter.

text.access_note: The exterior can be photographed from the open public square, but the church is a place of worship, so check the official site before you go if you want to go inside.

name: Henkersteg (Hangman's Bridge)
label: Henkersteg
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Maxbrücke' (5 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Maxbrücke' (way/476733337): middle (53 m across); moved 25 m off water.
pin_note: Position from OSM W137042471 (Hangman's Bridge): kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Covered wooden bridge with the Weinstadel and Wasserturm.

text.description:
The Henkersteg is a covered wooden footbridge over the Pegnitz in Nuremberg's Old Town. It is at its best as part of a group of buildings: the bridge itself, the round Henkerturm beside it, and the half-timbered Weinstadel with its water tower. Together they sit right on the river and make a compact, old-fashioned scene that suits a phone screen well.

The classic view is from the middle of the Maxbrücke, looking along the river toward the Henkersteg. From there the bridge, the tower and the Weinstadel line up against the water and the Old Town behind them. Several photography guides call this the postcard view, and say the Maxbrücke is a better place to photograph the Henkersteg than the Henkersteg itself. On a calm day the water beside the bridge can give a near-mirror reflection, which doubles the picture for no extra effort.

For a second angle, try Unschlittplatz on the land side. From there you see the Henkersteg and the Henkerturm up close, with the reflections of the historic facades in the Pegnitz.

Practical advice: stop in the middle of the Maxbrücke, but step to the side so you do not block people walking past. Turn on the gridlines so the river stays level, and take a few frames with the bridge on one side of the picture and the tower on the other. Then take one wider shot of the whole scene.
text.geographic_location: The Henkersteg is in Nuremberg's Old Town (Altstadt), crossing the Pegnitz river next to the Henkerturm and the Weinstadel.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so head for the Maxbrücke in the Old Town on foot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x), which holds the bridge, tower and Weinstadel together without stretching them. Use the telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for a tighter shot of the covered bridge and the tower. Keep the ultra-wide (0.5x) for Unschlittplatz, where you are close and need to fit in the facades. Keep the buildings away from the edges of an ultra-wide frame, as they can look bent there.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Maxbrücke (middle of the bridge, looking upstream toward the Henkersteg). The covered wooden Henkersteg, the Henkerturm, and the half-timbered Weinstadel with the water tower, framed against the Pegnitz and the Old Town. The Henkersteg is to the south from here. Unschlittplatz on the land side is a good alternative.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and place the water on the lower third, with the bridge and tower filling the middle. Hold the phone low, just above the parapet, so the reflection takes up more of the picture. Keep the horizon line level. For the second angle, go to Unschlittplatz and shoot the Henkersteg and Henkerturm from the land side, with the facades reflected in the river.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the old stonework or the timber to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky is bright, so the half-timbering keeps its detail. Wait for a calm moment on the water before pressing the shutter. A Live Photo can help you pick the frame with the cleanest reflection.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Choose a calm day, because still water gives the best reflection. Early in the day usually means fewer people on the bridge. Check how the light falls on the buildings when you arrive and take your time.

text.access_note: The Henkersteg is a public covered footbridge and the Maxbrücke is a public bridge, so you can photograph the scene from the street; for anything beyond that, check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: The Henkersteg is a public covered footbridge that is open at all times.
Calm days give the clearest reflections in the Pegnitz.
Early in the day there are usually fewer people on the Maxbrücke.
An ultra-wide lens can distort buildings near the edges of the frame.
The Henkersteg is about 1 minute on foot from the Maxbrücke viewpoint (56 m x 1.3 / 80 m per minute).
Standing on the Maxbrücke is a good place to stop briefly, if you stand to the side of foot traffic.

name: Frauenkirche
label: Frauenkirche
camera_source: Stand-here point set at the correction gate (own photo GPS 2026-11-16).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/143415043: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Frauenkirche' (57 m across).
notes: Gothic hall church on the Hauptmarkt with the Männleinlaufen clock.

text.description: The Frauenkirche, or Church of Our Lady, is a Gothic brick church on the eastern side of Nuremberg's main market, the Hauptmarkt. Emperor Charles IV had it built between 1352 and 1362, on the site of the synagogue that was demolished after the Jewish community was expelled in the wake of the Black Death. The architect was probably Peter Parler. It photographs well because the west front is so busy with detail. A deep porch with a balcony sits below a stepped gable with arcades, pinnacles and a small octagonal tower with a copper dome. The gable you see today dates from 1506 to 1508 and was designed by Adam Kraft. Above the porch is the Männleinlaufen, a mechanical clock from the early 1500s. At midday a bell rings, then trumpeters and a drummer appear, and the electors process around the figure of the Emperor. The balcony is also where the Christkindlesmarkt is opened each year. The church was almost completely destroyed in the Second World War, and its repairs were finished by 1953. Other sides of the church are quite plain, so concentrate on the west front.
text.geographic_location: In the old town of Nuremberg, on the eastern side of the Hauptmarkt (the main market square).
text.directions_text: There is no tram or railway stop right at this spot, so head for the Hauptmarkt in Nuremberg's old town, by taxi or hired scooter if you are coming from further away. The church stands on the eastern side of the square. The phone icon on the map is about 30 m south-west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole west front. Switch to the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the gable, the clock and the porch sculptures. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if crowds or stalls force you much closer.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 30 m south-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north-east. From there you can see the front and the gable together without leaning your phone far back.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and keep the central tower on the middle vertical line, with the phone held level so the vertical edges stay straight. Include a little of the square in the foreground to give a sense of scale. Then take a tighter shot of the clock and balcony using the telephoto.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest part of the stone to focus, then pull the exposure slider down slightly so the sky and pale facade keep their detail. Take a Live Photo around midday if you are catching the clock figures.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Around midday, when the Männleinlaufen clock performs. Afternoon or evening may suit the west front best for light, but the church can look good in most conditions.

text.access_note: The church is a Catholic parish church and its exterior is on a public square. Check the official site before you go for visiting arrangements inside, and be quiet and respectful if you step in.
general_notes: Because the church is on the eastern side of the market, a point 54 m to its south-west is probably in or beside the square, with a view of the west front.
At this distance the default lens (1x) should take in most of the west front, with the telephoto suited to details.
The west-facing front is likely to get more direct light in the afternoon and evening.
Crowds tend to gather around midday for the clock.
Visitors to churches are generally expected to behave quietly and respectfully.

name: Nuremberg Toy Museum
label: Toy Museum
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/4114977405: the OpenStreetMap point 'Gockelreiterbrunnen'.
notes: Museum of historic toys in the old town.

text.description: The Nuremberg Toy Museum fills the Hallersches Haus on Karlstraße, a house whose history goes back to 1517. The street side was rebuilt in 1611, and the oriel, a type called a chörlein, followed around 1720. The house was badly damaged in the Second World War and rebuilt afterwards. The museum opened here in 1971. For a quick phone photo, the best subject is the small Gockelreiterbrunnen (Rooster Rider Fountain) at the museum's front. Michael Mathias Prechtl designed it for the opening. A brightly painted ceramic rooster rider sits on a pipe above a concrete basin, held in by iron bars. It looks like a wooden toy, which suits the building behind it. The colours stand out well against the old façade, so one frame can show both the toy and the historic house. Inside, the collection has around 87,000 objects, though only a small share is on show at any time. It grew from the private collection of Lydia and Paul Bayer, which the city took over in 1966. Stand close to the fountain and use the rooster as the foreground. Let the oriel and the upper floors fill the background, and keep the bars and the basin edge in the frame for scale. Taking a second shot from a little further back lets you include more of the house. The museum is one of the stops on the Historical Mile Nuremberg, so you may be passing anyway.
text.geographic_location: The museum is at Karlstraße 13–15 in Nuremberg, and the rooster fountain stands in front of the museum. It is one of the stops on the Historical Mile Nuremberg.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so head for Karlstraße 13–15 in Nuremberg. If you are coming from further out, go by taxi or hired scooter and ask for the Spielzeugmuseum on Karlstraße. The fountain is right at the museum's front, and the phone icon on the map sits on it. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the fountain and the lower part of the house. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you cannot fit the whole façade. Use telephoto (2x–5x, depending on your phone) for the oriel and other details higher up.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Frame the rooster close up, with the house rising behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Put the painted rooster rider in the lower third of the frame and let the old house fill the rest. Turn on the gridlines and keep the vertical lines of the façade straight. Tilting the phone upwards makes the walls lean inwards, so hold it level and step back instead. Try a second shot with the rooster larger in the foreground and the oriel behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the rooster to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the bright colours stay strong and the sky does not wash out. Portrait mode can blur the background behind the figure, but check that the edges around the iron bars come out cleanly.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Daytime, when the colours of the figure show up best. Overcast light is fine, and it avoids harsh shadows.

text.access_note: The fountain stands outside at the museum's front. Check the museum's official site for opening and entry details before you go.

name: Fleisch Bridge
label: Fleischbrücke
camera_source: Stand-here point set at the correction gate (own photo GPS 2026-11-16).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/136788914: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Fleischbrücke' (32 m across).
notes: Stone bridge over the Pegnitz in the old town.

text.description:
The Fleisch Bridge, or "Meat Bridge", is a late Renaissance bridge over the river Pegnitz in the middle of Nuremberg's old town. It links the St. Sebald and St. Lorenz districts along the line of the main market. It photographs well because of its shape: a single, very flat stone arch, which gives a calm, simple curve over the water with old town buildings around it.

The bridge was built between 1596 and 1598 and replaced an earlier stone-and-wood bridge that floods kept destroying. At 15.3 m wide, with a clear span of 27 m, it was the largest masonry bridge arch in Germany when it was finished. The arch rises only 4.2 m, which is why it looks so flat. A portal was added in 1599, and the bridge has hardly changed since. It also came through the Second World War almost unscathed. The portal carries a Latin inscription about an ox that was never a calf, a small detail worth a close-up.

For a phone, think in two steps. Then walk closer for the arch, the portal and the inscription. Keep your phone level and switch on gridlines so the parapet and the water line stay straight. Tap on the stonework to set focus and pull the exposure slider down a touch if the sky is bright.
text.geographic_location: The Fleisch Bridge is in the centre of Nuremberg's old town, crossing the river Pegnitz between the St. Sebald and St. Lorenz districts. It sits on the axis of the main market.
text.directions_text: Head for Nuremberg's old town, close to the main market. From there the bridge is about 166 m on foot to the west. The phone icon on the map is about 160 m east of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: From where you stand, use the default lens (1x) for the bridge in its setting, or try telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to bring the arch closer. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) only when you are right next to the bridge.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 160 m east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face west.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on gridlines and line the arch up with the horizontal lines so the flat curve looks even. Include some of the river in the lower part of the frame to show how low and wide the arch is. Close to the bridge, a 0.5x shot along the parapet gives a sense of its width, and a 2x shot of the portal picks out the inscription.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the stonework to set focus, then lower the exposure slider slightly if the sky is washing out. Hold the phone steady against your body or a railing for sharper pictures.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft morning or late-afternoon light usually flatters stonework, and a quiet moment on the river gives the cleanest water. Check the light on the day, as shaded old town streets can be dim.

text.access_note: The bridge is part of the old town's main market axis, so it should be open to walk on, but check the official site before you go for any events or works.
claims_not_in_sources: Looking west from the stand-here point, the bridge and river should be in view, though buildings or trees may block part of the view.
Morning or late-afternoon light is usually softer on stonework.
A calm river surface gives a cleaner view of the water beneath the arch.
The bridge is open to pedestrians as part of the public street.
The bridge is at a distance where a 2x-5x telephoto helps.

name: Albrecht Dürer's House
label: Dürer House
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Sinwellturm' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Sinwellturm' (way/23448852): middle (17 m across); moved 10 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/32477251: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Albrecht Dürer's House' (34 m across).
notes: Half-timbered home of the painter below the castle.

text.description: Albrecht Dürer's House is a tall, half-timbered townhouse in the north-west corner of Nuremberg's old town, close to the castle and the city wall. Dürer lived here from 1509 until his death in 1528. The house dates from around 1420 and has five storeys. The lower two are sandstone, the upper ones are timber-framed, and a half-hip roof sits on top. It has been a museum about Dürer since 1871. It was badly damaged by bombing in October 1944, rebuilt by 1949 and reopened as a museum in 1971. It photographs well because the pale stonework, dark timbers and steep roof make a clear shape, and the setting is full of character. The most unusual angle is from above, looking down on the roof and facade from the city wall walkway near the Tiergärtnertor. This is usually quieter than the square in front. If you would rather stay at street level, Tiergärtnertorplatz gives you the facade with the bronze Dürer monument in front and the castle rising behind. Albrecht-Dürer-Straße gives a framed view down the cobbled street. Keep your phone level so the timber lines stay straight, and take a few frames at different zoom levels so you can choose later.
text.geographic_location: In the extreme north-west of Nuremberg's Altstadt (old town), near the Kaiserburg castle and the Tiergärtnertor in the city walls.
text.directions_text: No tram or railway stop is listed for this spot, so head for the Kaiserburg and Tiergärtnertor area in the north-west of the Altstadt. Check on site that the wall walkway is open before you try to climb up for the higher view. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the telephoto lens (2x-5x, depending on your phone) from a higher viewpoint, such as the wall, to pick out the roof and facade. Switch to the default lens (1x) to include the surrounding rooftops. At street level, the ultra-wide (0.5x) helps in the narrow street or the square.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at Sinwellturm (on the city wall walkway near the Tiergärtnertor). An elevated view looking down onto the house's roof and facade from the city wall.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the roof ridge up with one of them, so the building does not lean. Leave a little of the neighbouring roofs in the frame to show the house's place in the old town. If the wall is closed, try Tiergärtnertorplatz for the facade with the bronze monument and castle behind, or Albrecht-Dürer-Straße for the house framed by the cobbled street.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the facade to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the bright sandstone and sky do not wash out. Take a 1x shot and a zoomed shot from the same spot.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft morning or late-afternoon light is kinder to the timber and stonework than harsh midday sun.

text.access_note: The house is a museum, and access to the Sinwellturm and the city wall walkway can vary, so check the official site and on-site signs before you go, including any rules on photography inside.

name: Nassau House
label: Nassauer Haus
camera_source: Stand-here point set at the correction gate (own photo GPS 2026-11-16).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/32397234: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Nassauer Haus' (15 m across).
notes: Medieval tower-like townhouse on Lorenzer Platz.

text.description: Nassau House is a stout, reddish stone tower on a street corner in the old town, and it looks quite unlike anything around it. It is the last surviving medieval residential tower in Nuremberg. Around 1430 there are said to have been about 65 of them. The cellar and two lower floors date from the 13th century, and the two upper floors were added in the 15th century. It began as a Romanesque building but now looks mostly Gothic. For a phone photo, the best part is the top: a frieze of coats of arms runs beneath the roof, with three small pointed-roofed corner turrets and a pyramid-shaped roof above. The building was badly damaged in 1945 and rebuilt between 1950 and 1954. Much of the frieze was renewed then, and only the left-hand turret is original. The name 'Nassau House' has only been used since the 19th century and rests on a mistaken link to a medieval German king. The contrast between the small-scale masonry of the lower floors and the neat, regular blocks of the upper floors makes a good detail shot. The tower is tall and sits on a corner, so you will need to stand back and tilt the phone upwards, which can make the walls lean inwards. Keep the phone as level as you can, use the gridlines to line up the corner, and let the turrets and frieze fill the top of the frame.
text.geographic_location: Nassau House stands in Nuremberg's Lorenzer Altstadt, at Karolinenstraße 2, opposite the Lorenzkirche.
text.directions_text: Head for the Lorenzer Altstadt and the Lorenzkirche, by taxi or hired scooter if you are coming from further away. The tower is directly opposite the church. The phone icon on the map is about 65 m east of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole tower. Switch to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the coat of arms frieze and the turrets. Use ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you have to stand very close, and expect the walls to lean.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 65 m east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face west.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and line a vertical edge of the corner up with one of them to keep the walls straight. Leave a little sky above the roof. Then zoom in for a second shot of the frieze and the pointed turrets. For a close-up, use the change from small lower stonework to the neat upper blocks.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the sunlit stone to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky does not wash out and the red sandstone keeps its colour. Hold the phone steady with both hands when zoomed in.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft light, either on an overcast day or later in the afternoon, tends to show the texture of the sandstone best and avoids harsh shadows across the frieze.

text.access_note: The outside can be photographed from the street. The cellar is used as an inn and the tower is owned by a foundation, so check the official site before you go if you want to see inside.

name: Nuremberg Town Hall
label: Rathaus
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Hauptmarkt' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Hauptmarkt' (way/136698909): middle (181 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/1841447: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Altes Rathaus' (106 m across).
notes: Large old town hall between the Sebalduskirche and the castle.

text.description: Nuremberg's Town Hall is a long Renaissance building in the old town, and it photographs well because its design is so distinctive. A uniform front of windows is broken by three Baroque portals, and little 'dwarf houses' stand up in the roofline. The main building was put up between 1616 and 1622 to designs by Jakob Wolff the Younger. Its oldest part, the great hall on the south side, dates from 1332–1340. The whole complex burned down to its outer walls in 1944–45, and the Old Town Hall was rebuilt between 1956 and 1962, so what you see today is a careful rebuilding. On the market-square side stands the 1950s New Town Hall, whose angled layout leaves a view through to the southern tower of the old building. That gap makes a nice detail shot. The best all-round picture is from the Hauptmarkt, where the Schöner Brunnen fountain stands beside the Town Hall and the Frauenkirche is close by. Put the fountain in the foreground and let the Town Hall sit behind it. Expect other visitors in the frame, so be patient and take a few shots.
text.geographic_location: In the old town (Altstadt) of Nuremberg, just east of the choir of the Sebalduskirche, with the Hauptmarkt on its market-square side.
text.directions_text: Make your way to the old town and the Hauptmarkt. For the alternative view, continue to the Rathausplatz beside the Old Town Hall. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the fountain and Town Hall together. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want a close fountain in the foreground. Use telephoto (2x–5x, depending on your phone) for the portals and roofline details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Hauptmarkt. The Rathaus as part of a backdrop on the main market square, with the Schöner Brunnen fountain beside it and the Frauenkirche nearby.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line up the long roofline with a horizontal grid line. Put the fountain low in the frame as a foreground element, and leave the Town Hall as the backdrop. For a different view, the Rathausplatz shows the Old Town Hall on one side and the Sebalduskirche towers on the other, looking north across the square.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest part of the sky or facade and lower the exposure slider a little, so the stonework keeps its detail. At 0.5x, keep the building well away from the edges of the frame so the lines don't lean.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or later in the day will usually mean fewer people in the square. Take a few shots in case someone walks through.

text.access_note: The Hauptmarkt is an open public square, but access to the Town Hall interior and any tours or cellars may be ticketed or restricted, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Early morning or later in the day usually means fewer people on the Hauptmarkt.
An ultra-wide lens can make vertical lines lean if the building is near the edge of the frame.
Lowering the exposure slider helps keep detail in bright stonework and sky.
